optWhy.A: Correct: negative stereotypes and distrust fuel intergroup hostility.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: these are negative, not positive, relations.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: conflict is present.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: these are group-level processes, not only individual liking.

stem: Collective identity in conflict can intensify intergroup hostility when:

options.text: Group members strongly identify with their in-group and view the out-group as a threat.

why: Collective identity intensifies intergroup hostility when members strongly identify with their in-group and view the out-group as a threat; it is not absence of identification, only individual identity, or absence of conflict.

optWhy.A: Correct: strong in-group identification plus out-group threat intensifies hostility.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: group identification is present.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: collective identity is a group-level process.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: conflict is present.

stem: Collective narcissism refers to:

options.text: An unrealistic belief in one's group's greatness combined with sensitivity to perceived slights against the group.
Accurate recognition of one's group's achievements.

why: Collective narcissism is an unrealistic belief in one's group's greatness combined with sensitivity to perceived slights against the group; it is not accurate recognition, low identification, or humility.

optWhy.A: Correct: collective narcissism is unrealistic group greatness plus sensitivity to slights.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: collective narcissism is unrealistic, not accurate.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: collective narcissism involves high, not low, identification.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: collective narcissism is not humility.

stem: Peace education aims to:

options.text: Develop knowledge, skills, and attitudes for building peace and resolving conflict non-violently.

why: Peace education aims to develop knowledge, skills, and attitudes for building peace and resolving conflict non-violently; it is not only military history, promoting violence, or ignoring social context.

optWhy.A: Correct: peace education develops knowledge, skills, and attitudes for peace and non-violent conflict resolution.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: peace education is not only military history.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: peace education opposes violence.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: peace education considers social context.

stem: A school programme teaches students communication, empathy, and conflict-resolution skills to reduce bullying and promote cooperation. This reflects:

options.text: Peace education developing skills for non-violent conflict resolution and cooperation.

why: Teaching communication, empathy, and conflict-resolution skills to reduce bullying and promote cooperation reflects peace education developing skills for non-violent conflict resolution and cooperation; it is not only punishment, promoting hostility, or ignoring bullying.

optWhy.A: Correct: communication, empathy, and conflict-resolution skills are peace education.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: peace education is broader than only punishment.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: peace education reduces, not promotes, hostility.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: bullying is addressed, not ignored.

stem: Match each peace-education component (List-I) with its purpose (List-II).
listII: Students work together toward shared goals.
Intergroup contact under favourable conditions reduces prejudice.
Parties learn to negotiate and resolve disputes non-violently.
why: Contact-based programmes → intergroup contact under favourable conditions reduces prejudice (2); Cooperative learning → students work together toward shared goals (1); Conflict-resolution training → parties learn to negotiate and resolve disputes non-violently (3). Thus Contact-based-2, Cooperative learning-1, Conflict-resolution training-3.

optWhy.A: Correct: Contact-based-2, Cooperative learning-1, Conflict-resolution training-3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Contact-based-1 wrongly assigns shared goals to contact-based programmes.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Contact-based-3 wrongly assigns negotiation to contact-based programmes.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Cooperative learning-3 wrongly assigns negotiation to cooperative learning.

stem: Two signatory groups negotiate a power-sharing agreement after civil war. This reflects:

options.text: Macro-level conflict resolution through a peace agreement and power-sharing.

why: Negotiating a power-sharing agreement after civil war reflects macro-level conflict resolution through a peace agreement and power-sharing; it is not only individual therapy, absence of agreement, or renewed violence.

optWhy.A: Correct: power-sharing agreement after civil war is macro-level conflict resolution.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: macro-level is societal, not only individual therapy.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: an agreement is present.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the agreement aims to end, not renew, violence.

stem: Post-conflict reconstruction involves:

options.text: Rebuilding institutions, infrastructure, and social relationships after conflict.

why: Post-conflict reconstruction involves rebuilding institutions, infrastructure, and social relationships after conflict; it is not only punishment, restarting conflict, or ignoring the aftermath.

optWhy.A: Correct: rebuilding institutions, infrastructure, and social relationships.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: reconstruction is broader than only punishment.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: reconstruction ends, not restarts, conflict.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the aftermath is addressed, not ignored.

stem: Media framing in conflict can influence escalation by:

options.text: Selectively emphasising certain aspects of the conflict, shaping how audiences interpret it.
Having no effect on audience interpretation.

why: Media framing can influence conflict escalation by selectively emphasising certain aspects of the conflict and shaping audience interpretation; it is not without effect, always de-escalating, or only positive.

optWhy.A: Correct: media framing selectively emphasises aspects and shapes interpretation.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: media framing does affect interpretation.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: media framing can escalate or de-escalate, not always de-escalate.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: media framing is not only positive.

stem: Propaganda, misinformation, and hate speech in conflict can:

options.text: Fuel prejudice, dehumanisation, and intergroup hostility.

why: Propaganda, misinformation, and hate speech in conflict can fuel prejudice, dehumanisation, and intergroup hostility; they do not always promote peace, have no effect, or only target individuals.

optWhy.A: Correct: propaganda, misinformation, and hate speech fuel prejudice, dehumanisation, and intergroup hostility.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: they do not always promote peace.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: they affect attitudes.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: they target groups, not only individuals.

stem: Peace journalism differs from conventional war journalism by:

options.text: Reporting on causes, perspectives of all parties, and peace initiatives rather than only violence.

why: Peace journalism reports on causes, perspectives of all parties, and peace initiatives rather than only violence; it is not only violence, always taking one side, or ignoring the conflict.

optWhy.A: Correct: peace journalism covers causes, all perspectives, and peace initiatives.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: peace journalism is broader than only violence.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: peace journalism includes all perspectives, not one side.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: peace journalism addresses the conflict.

stem: Consider the following statements about media and conflict:
statements: Media framing can shape how audiences interpret a conflict.
Propaganda and hate speech can fuel intergroup hostility.
Peace journalism reports only on violence and ignores causes.
Peace initiatives and multiple perspectives can be part of conflict coverage.
why: Statement 1 is true (framing shapes interpretation); statement 2 is true (propaganda and hate speech fuel hostility); statement 3 is false (peace journalism reports on causes and multiple perspectives, not only violence); statement 4 is true (peace initiatives and multiple perspectives can be part of coverage). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: Members of two conflicting communities engage in facilitated dialogue to share experiences and rebuild trust. This reflects:
why: Facilitated dialogue to share experiences and rebuild trust reflects intergroup dialogue for reconciliation; it is not escalation, absence of conflict, or only debate to win.

optWhy.A: Correct: facilitated dialogue to share experiences and rebuild trust is intergroup dialogue for reconciliation.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: dialogue de-escalates, not escalates.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: conflicting communities are present.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: dialogue aims at understanding, not winning.

stem: Truth and reconciliation processes after mass violence typically involve:

options.text: Acknowledging harms, establishing facts, and working toward restored relationships.
Erasing all memory of the violence.

why: Truth and reconciliation processes involve acknowledging harms, establishing facts, and working toward restored relationships; they are not erasing memory, only punishment, or continuing hostilities.

optWhy.A: Correct: acknowledging harms, establishing facts, and restoring relationships.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: truth processes preserve, not erase, memory.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: truth and reconciliation is broader than only punishment.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: reconciliation ends hostilities.

stem: Consider the following statements about collective violence and intergroup conflict:
statements: Collective violence is committed by a group or collectivity.
Dehumanisation facilitates collective violence by removing moral consideration.
Intergroup conflict is always violent.
Scapegoating and a devaluing ideology can contribute to genocide.
why: Statement 1 is true (collective violence is by a group); statement 2 is true (dehumanisation facilitates violence); statement 3 is false (intergroup conflict is not always violent); statement 4 is true (scapegoating and devaluing ideology contribute to genocide). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Reconciliation after conflict involves rebuilding trust between former adversaries.
reason: Trust is damaged during conflict and must be deliberately restored for reconciliation.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

why: Assertion A is true: reconciliation after conflict involves rebuilding trust between former adversaries. Reason R is true: trust is damaged during conflict and must be deliberately restored for reconciliation. R correctly explains A.

optWhy.A: Correct: both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: R is the correct explanation of A.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: R is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: A is true.

stem: After a peace-education programme, students show greater empathy toward the out-group and use non-violent strategies to resolve disagreements. These are:
why: Greater empathy toward the out-group and use of non-violent strategies are intended outcomes of peace education; they are not evidence of failure, increased hostility, or no change.

optWhy.A: Correct: greater empathy and non-violent strategies are intended peace-education outcomes.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: these indicate success, not failure.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: hostility decreased, not increased.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: attitudes changed toward empathy.

stem: Consider the following statements about macro-level conflict resolution:
statements: Peace agreements can end formal hostilities.
Power-sharing arrangements distribute political authority among groups.
Post-conflict reconstruction is unnecessary after a peace agreement.
Macro-level resolution addresses societal structures and institutions.
why: Statement 1 is true (peace agreements can end hostilities); statement 2 is true (power-sharing distributes political authority); statement 3 is false (post-conflict reconstruction is necessary after an agreement); statement 4 is true (macro-level resolution addresses societal structures and institutions). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A news outlet repeatedly shows only one side's suffering and uses dehumanising language about the other side. This media coverage is likely to:

options.text: Escalate conflict by fueling prejudice and dehumanisation.

why: Showing only one side's suffering and using dehumanising language about the other side is likely to escalate conflict by fueling prejudice and dehumanisation; it is not de-escalating, without effect, or balanced.

optWhy.A: Correct: one-sided suffering coverage and dehumanising language escalate conflict.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: this coverage escalates, not de-escalates.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: media coverage affects attitudes.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: only one side is shown, so it is not balanced.

stem: Consider the following statements about the contact hypothesis:
statements: Intergroup contact reduces prejudice under favourable conditions.
Equal status and common goals are favourable contact conditions.
Any contact, including hostile contact, reduces prejudice.
Institutional support is a favourable contact condition.
why: Statement 1 is true (contact reduces prejudice under favourable conditions); statement 2 is true (equal status and common goals are favourable); statement 3 is false (hostile contact does not reduce prejudice); statement 4 is true (institutional support is favourable). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A study compares two intervention communities: Community P receives contact-based programmes under favourable conditions (equal status, cooperation, institutional support), while Community Q receives no intervention. After six months, Community P shows lower intergroup prejudice and higher trust. The best-supported conclusion is:

options.text: Contact-based programmes under favourable conditions are associated with lower prejudice and higher trust than no intervention.

why: The best-supported conclusion is that contact-based programmes under favourable conditions are associated with lower prejudice and higher trust than no intervention; it does not show contact always eliminates prejudice, no intervention produces lower prejudice, prejudice is unaffected, or only hostile contact matters.

optWhy.A: Correct: Community P (favourable contact) shows lower prejudice and higher trust than Community Q (no intervention).
optWhy.B: Incorrect: contact does not always eliminate prejudice.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Community Q (no intervention) did not produce lower prejudice.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: prejudice differed by intervention, so it is affected.

stem: Wellbeing is best understood as:

options.text: A multidimensional state encompassing psychological, social, and emotional wellbeing.
Only the absence of mental illness.
A fixed trait that cannot change.

why: Wellbeing is a multidimensional state encompassing psychological, social, and emotional wellbeing; it is not only the absence of mental illness, only financial wealth, or a fixed unchangeable trait.

optWhy.A: Correct: wellbeing is multidimensional — psychological, social, and emotional.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: wellbeing is broader than only the absence of mental illness.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: financial wealth is only one possible contributor.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: wellbeing can change over time.

stem: Hedonic wellbeing emphasises:

options.text: Pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction (subjective wellbeing).
Only meaning and purpose in life.
The absence of all negative emotion.

why: Hedonic wellbeing emphasises pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction, captured by subjective wellbeing (Diener); it is not only meaning/purpose, absence of all negative emotion, or only virtue.

optWhy.A: Correct: hedonic wellbeing is pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: meaning and purpose characterise eudaimonic wellbeing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: hedonic wellbeing does not require absence of all negative emotion.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: virtue and moral excellence are not the focus of hedonic wellbeing.

stem: Eudaimonic wellbeing emphasises:

options.text: Meaning, purpose, self-realisation, and psychological flourishing.

why: Eudaimonic wellbeing emphasises meaning, purpose, self-realisation, and psychological flourishing (Ryff); it is not only pleasure/positive affect, financial success, or absence of all challenges.

optWhy.A: Correct: eudaimonic wellbeing is meaning, purpose, self-realisation, and flourishing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: pleasure and positive affect characterise hedonic wellbeing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: financial success is not the focus of eudaimonic wellbeing.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: eudaimonic wellbeing does not require absence of all challenges.

stem: A person pursues a meaningful career that involves long hours and occasional stress because it aligns with their values and sense of purpose. This reflects:

options.text: Eudaimonic wellbeing, centred on meaning and purpose.

why: Pursuing a meaningful, values-aligned career despite occasional stress reflects eudaimonic wellbeing (meaning and purpose); it is not only hedonic wellbeing, absence of stress, or low wellbeing.

optWhy.A: Correct: meaning and purpose-driven pursuit is eudaimonic wellbeing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: hedonic wellbeing centres on pleasure and positive affect, not meaning.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: eudaimonic wellbeing can coexist with occasional stress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: meaning-aligned pursuit indicates wellbeing, not low wellbeing.

stem: Diener's subjective wellbeing differs from Ryff's psychological wellbeing in that subjective wellbeing centres on:

options.text: Life satisfaction, positive affect, and low negative affect (the person's own evaluation).

why: Diener's subjective wellbeing centres on life satisfaction, positive affect, and low negative affect — the person's own evaluation; Ryff's psychological wellbeing centres on six dimensions including autonomy and purpose. Subjective wellbeing is not only autonomy/mastery, only meaning/purpose, or objective indicators.

optWhy.A: Correct: subjective wellbeing is life satisfaction, positive affect, low negative affect — the person's evaluation.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: autonomy and environmental mastery are Ryff's psychological wellbeing dimensions.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: meaning and purpose are eudaimonic/psychological wellbeing, not the whole of subjective wellbeing.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: subjective wellbeing is the person's own evaluation, not objective indicators.

stem: Match each Ryff dimension of psychological wellbeing (List-I) with its description (List-II).
listII: The capacity to manage one's life and surroundings effectively.
Continued development and realisation of potential.
Warm, satisfying, trusting relationships.
Self-determination and independence.

options.text: Autonomy-4, Environmental mastery-1, Personal growth-2, Positive relations-3
Autonomy-1, Environmental mastery-2, Personal growth-3, Positive relations-4
Autonomy-3, Environmental mastery-4, Personal growth-1, Personal growth-2
Autonomy-2, Environmental mastery-3, Personal growth-4, Positive relations-1

why: Autonomy = self-determination and independence (4); Environmental mastery = capacity to manage one's life and surroundings (1); Personal growth = continued development and realisation of potential (2); Positive relations with others = warm, satisfying, trusting relationships (3). Thus Autonomy-4, Environmental mastery-1, Personal growth-2, Positive relations-3.

optWhy.A: Correct: Autonomy-4, Environmental mastery-1, Personal growth-2, Positive relations-3.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Autonomy-1 wrongly assigns life management to autonomy.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Autonomy-3 wrongly assigns relationships to autonomy.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Autonomy-2 wrongly assigns development to autonomy.

stem: Seligman's PERMA model of wellbeing includes:

options.text: Positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment.

why: Seligman's PERMA model includes Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, and Accomplishment; it is not only pleasure/life satisfaction, only meaning/purpose, or only income/health.

optWhy.A: Correct: PERMA is Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning, Accomplishment.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: only pleasure and life satisfaction is hedonic/subjective wellbeing, not PERMA.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: only meaning and purpose is not the full PERMA model.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: income and health are not the PERMA elements.

stem: Hedonic adaptation (the hedonic treadmill) suggests that:

options.text: People tend to return to a relatively stable baseline of wellbeing after positive or negative events.
Wellbeing permanently rises after every positive event.
Wellbeing permanently falls after every negative event.
Wellbeing is unaffected by life events.

why: Hedonic adaptation suggests people return to a relatively stable baseline of wellbeing after positive or negative events; wellbeing does not permanently rise after every positive event, permanently fall after every negative event, or remain unaffected.

optWhy.A: Correct: hedonic adaptation is return to a stable baseline after events.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: wellbeing does not permanently rise after every positive event.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: wellbeing does not permanently fall after every negative event.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: life events affect wellbeing, at least temporarily.

stem: Keyes's complete mental health model distinguishes flourishing from languishing, where flourishing:

options.text: Combines high wellbeing with low mental illness.
Is the same as the absence of mental illness.

why: Keyes's model defines flourishing as high wellbeing combined with low mental illness; it is not the same as absence of mental illness, does not require high mental illness, and is not only financial success.

optWhy.A: Correct: flourishing is high wellbeing with low mental illness.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: flourishing is more than absence of mental illness.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: flourishing does not require high mental illness.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: flourishing is not only financial success.

stem: Consider the following statements about wellbeing models:
statements: Hedonic wellbeing centres on pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction.
Eudaimonic wellbeing centres on meaning, purpose, and self-realisation.
Diener's subjective wellbeing and Ryff's psychological wellbeing are identical constructs.
Seligman's PERMA includes positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment.
why: Statement 1 is true (hedonic wellbeing); statement 2 is true (eudaimonic wellbeing); statement 3 is false (Diener's subjective wellbeing and Ryff's psychological wellbeing are related but distinct constructs); statement 4 is true (PERMA elements). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A person reports high life satisfaction, frequent positive affect, and infrequent negative affect. This profile reflects:
why: High life satisfaction, frequent positive affect, and infrequent negative affect reflect high subjective wellbeing; they are not low subjective wellbeing, only eudaimonic wellbeing, or absence of emotion.

optWhy.A: Correct: high life satisfaction, positive affect, low negative affect = high subjective wellbeing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: this profile indicates high, not low, subjective wellbeing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: this is the subjective wellbeing profile, not only eudaimonic wellbeing.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: affect is present, not absent.

stem: Peterson and Seligman's VIA classification identifies character strengths such as:
why: The VIA classification (Peterson & Seligman) identifies 24 character strengths under six virtues, including curiosity, kindness, fairness, and perseverance; it is not only financial ambition, physical fitness, or IQ.

optWhy.A: Correct: curiosity, kindness, fairness, and perseverance are VIA character strengths.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: financial ambition is not a VIA character strength.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: physical fitness is not a VIA character strength.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: IQ is not a VIA character strength.

stem: A person who frequently uses their top character strengths in daily life is described as using:
why: Frequently using one's top character strengths in daily life describes using signature strengths; it is not weaknesses, only acquired skills, or character deficits.

optWhy.A: Correct: frequently used top strengths are signature strengths.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: strengths are not weaknesses.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: signature strengths are character strengths, not only acquired skills.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: using strengths is not a deficit.

stem: Positive psychology, per Seligman, studies:

options.text: What makes life most worth living, including strengths, wellbeing, and flourishing.

why: Positive psychology studies what makes life most worth living, including strengths, wellbeing, and flourishing; it is not only mental illness, only financial success, or absence of all emotion.

optWhy.A: Correct: positive psychology studies strengths, wellbeing, and flourishing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: positive psychology is not only mental illness.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: financial success is not the sole focus.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: emotion is present, not absent.

stem: Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory proposes that positive emotions:

options.text: Broaden thought-action repertoires and build enduring personal resources.
Only narrow attention to immediate threats.

why: Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory proposes that positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoires and build enduring personal resources; they do not only narrow attention to threats, always eliminate negative emotions, or have no effect.

optWhy.A: Correct: positive emotions broaden thought-action repertoires and build resources.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: narrowing attention to threats is associated with negative emotions.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: positive emotions do not always eliminate negative emotions.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: positive emotions build resources.

stem: A person feels satisfied with life, experiences frequent positive emotions, has warm relationships, pursues meaningful goals, and feels competent in managing daily life. This profile best reflects:

options.text: High wellbeing across hedonic and eudaimonic dimensions.

why: Life satisfaction and positive emotions (hedonic) plus warm relationships, meaningful goals, and competence (eudaimonic) reflect high wellbeing across both dimensions; it is not low wellbeing, only financial wealth, or absence of challenge.

optWhy.A: Correct: the profile combines hedonic (satisfaction, positive emotion) and eudaimonic (relationships, meaning, competence) wellbeing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the profile indicates high wellbeing.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: financial wealth is not the sole indicator.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: wellbeing does not require absence of challenge.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing are distinct but related constructs.
reason: Hedonic wellbeing centres on pleasure and life satisfaction, whereas eudaimonic wellbeing centres on meaning and self-realisation.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

why: Assertion A is true: hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing are distinct but related constructs. Reason R is true: hedonic wellbeing centres on pleasure and life satisfaction; eudaimonic wellbeing centres on meaning and self-realisation. R correctly explains A.

optWhy.A: Correct: both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: R is the correct explanation of A.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: R is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: A is true.

stem: A study randomly assigns participants to either a gratitude-journaling condition or a control condition for six weeks, then measures life satisfaction. The gratitude group reports significantly higher life satisfaction. The best-supported conclusion is:

options.text: Gratitude journaling is associated with higher life satisfaction than the control condition.
Gratitude journaling permanently cures low wellbeing.
Journaling has no effect on wellbeing.

why: The best-supported conclusion is that gratitude journaling is associated with higher life satisfaction than the control condition; it does not show permanent cure, that controls have higher wellbeing, that journaling has no effect, or that only negative emotions matter.

optWhy.A: Correct: gratitude journaling is associated with higher life satisfaction than control.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the study does not show permanent cure.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the gratitude group, not controls, reported higher satisfaction.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the gratitude group reported higher satisfaction, so journaling had an effect.

stem: In the Indian context, wellbeing may be understood through:

options.text: Both psychological/social dimensions and culturally relevant concepts such as family harmony and spiritual well-being.
The absence of any cultural influence.

why: In the Indian context, wellbeing may be understood through psychological/social dimensions plus culturally relevant concepts such as family harmony and spiritual well-being; it is not only Western individualistic measures, only income, or devoid of cultural influence.

optWhy.A: Correct: Indian wellbeing includes psychological/social dimensions plus family harmony and spiritual well-being.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: wellbeing is not only Western individualistic measures.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: income is not the only indicator.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: culture influences wellbeing.

stem: Consider the following statements about wellbeing and flourishing:
statements: Flourishing combines high wellbeing with good mental health.
Languishing is low wellbeing even without a mental illness.
Wellbeing is fixed and cannot be enhanced.
Positive emotions can build enduring personal resources.
why: Statement 1 is true (flourishing combines high wellbeing with good mental health); statement 2 is true (languishing is low wellbeing even without mental illness); statement 3 is false (wellbeing can be enhanced); statement 4 is true (positive emotions build resources per broaden-and-build). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: Match each wellbeing tradition (List-I) with its core focus (List-II).
listII: Meaning, purpose, self-realisation, and flourishing.
Pleasure, positive affect, and life satisfaction.
why: Hedonic wellbeing → pleasure, positive affect, life satisfaction (2); Eudaimonic wellbeing → meaning, purpose, self-realisation, flourishing (1). Thus Hedonic-2, Eudaimonic-1.

optWhy.A: Correct: Hedonic-2, Eudaimonic-1.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: this reverses the traditions.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: both assigned to eudaimonic focus.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: both assigned to hedonic focus.

stem: Read Assertion (A) and Reason (R), then choose the correct option.
assertion: Wellbeing can change over time and be enhanced through intentional activities.
reason: Wellbeing is a fixed trait determined only at birth.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

why: Assertion A is true: wellbeing can change over time and be enhanced through intentional activities. Reason R is false: wellbeing is not a fixed trait determined only at birth. Since A is true and R is false, code C applies.

optWhy.A: Incorrect: R is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: R is false.
optWhy.C: Correct: A is true but R is false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: A is true, not false.

stem: Consider the following statements about wellbeing measurement:
statements: Subjective wellbeing is based on the person's own evaluation.
Psychological wellbeing uses multidimensional criteria such as autonomy and purpose.
Wellbeing can be captured fully by income alone.
Hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing can coexist.
why: Statement 1 is true (subjective wellbeing is self-evaluation); statement 2 is true (psychological wellbeing uses multidimensional criteria); statement 3 is false (wellbeing cannot be captured fully by income alone); statement 4 is true (hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing can coexist). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A workplace programme identifies employees' signature strengths and designs roles to use them. This reflects:
why: Identifying signature strengths and designing roles to use them reflects a strengths-based positive-psychology application; it is not only correcting weaknesses, ignoring wellbeing, or a medical treatment.

optWhy.A: Correct: identifying and using signature strengths is a strengths-based application.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the programme focuses on strengths, not only weaknesses.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: employee wellbeing is addressed.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: this is not a medical treatment.

stem: Consider the following statements about wellbeing:
statements: Hedonic wellbeing concerns pleasure and life satisfaction.
Eudaimonic wellbeing concerns meaning and self-realisation.
Diener's subjective wellbeing is the only valid wellbeing construct.
Flourishing involves high wellbeing and low mental illness.
why: Statement 1 is true (hedonic wellbeing); statement 2 is true (eudaimonic wellbeing); statement 3 is false (Diener's subjective wellbeing is not the only valid construct); statement 4 is true (flourishing involves high wellbeing and low mental illness). Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correct.

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: Resilience is best defined as:

options.text: The capacity to adapt well in the face of adversity, trauma, or significant stress.
A fixed trait that cannot change.

why: Resilience is the capacity to adapt well in the face of adversity, trauma, or significant stress.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilience is the capacity to adapt well in the face of adversity.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilience is not the absence of adversity.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilient people can still experience distress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not a fixed unchangeable trait.

stem: Masten's description of resilience as "ordinary magic" means that:

options.text: Resilience arises from ordinary protective processes such as supportive relationships and effective coping.
Resilience is only for the exceptionally strong.

why: Masten's 'ordinary magic' means resilience arises from ordinary protective processes such as supportive relationships and effective coping.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilience arises from ordinary protective processes.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilience is not rare and extraordinary.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilience does not require supernatural abilities.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not only for the exceptionally strong.

stem: Resilience can be understood as:

options.text: An outcome, a process, or a capacity that varies across contexts.

why: Resilience can be understood as an outcome, a process, or a capacity that varies across contexts.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilience is outcome, process, or capacity varying across contexts.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilience is not only a fixed trait.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilience is not only absence of stress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not only genetic inheritance.

stem: Protective factors in resilience:

options.text: Reduce the likelihood of poor outcomes in the face of risk.
Are the same as risk factors.
Guarantee good outcomes in every case.

why: Protective factors reduce the likelihood of poor outcomes in the face of risk.

optWhy.A: Correct: protective factors reduce the likelihood of poor outcomes in the face of risk.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: protective factors are not the same as risk factors.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: protective factors do not guarantee good outcomes in every case.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: protective factors operate across the lifespan.

stem: A community that organises mutual aid after a natural disaster, supporting members and rebuilding together, demonstrates:
why: Mutual aid and collective rebuilding after a disaster demonstrate community resilience.

optWhy.A: Correct: mutual aid and collective rebuilding demonstrate community resilience.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the disaster occurred.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: community resilience is collective, not only individual coping.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience can change and grow.

stem: Resilience develops through:

options.text: The interaction of individual characteristics with supportive relationships and environmental resources over time.

why: Resilience develops through the interaction of individual characteristics with supportive relationships and environmental resources over time.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilience develops through interaction of individual characteristics with supportive relationships and environmental resources.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilience is not only genetic inheritance.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilience is not only absence of adversity.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not a single traumatic event.

stem: A person who loses their job but uses social support, problem-solving, and meaning-making to adapt and find new work demonstrates:

options.text: Resilience in the face of adversity.

why: Using social support, problem-solving, and meaning-making to adapt after job loss demonstrates resilience in the face of adversity.

optWhy.A: Correct: using support, problem-solving, and meaning-making to adapt is resilience.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the person likely experiences stress but copes.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the person copes and finds new work.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not genetic determinism.

stem: A family that maintains routines, communicates openly, and draws on extended kin support during a crisis demonstrates:
why: Maintaining routines, open communication, and drawing on kin support during a crisis demonstrate family resilience.

optWhy.A: Correct: routines, communication, and kin support demonstrate family resilience.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the crisis occurred.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: family resilience is collective, not only individual coping.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: family resilience can change and grow.

sub: Resilience not the absence of distress
stem: Resilient individuals:

options.text: May experience distress but can adapt and recover over time.

why: Resilient individuals may experience distress but can adapt and recover over time; they are not unaffected by adversity.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilient individuals may experience distress but adapt and recover.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilient individuals can experience distress.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilient individuals are affected by adversity.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilient individuals have emotional reactions.

stem: Post-traumatic growth refers to:

options.text: Positive psychological change experienced as a result of struggling with highly challenging life circumstances.

why: Post-traumatic growth is positive psychological change experienced as a result of struggling with highly challenging life circumstances.

optWhy.A: Correct: post-traumatic growth is positive change from struggling with highly challenging circumstances.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: post-traumatic growth follows trauma, not its absence.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: it is positive change, not only distress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: it is not guaranteed for everyone.

stem: Match each PTGI domain (List-I) with its description (List-II).
listII: A greater sense of one's own inner strength and capability.
Recognising new paths and opportunities in life.
Deepened and more meaningful relationships.
A heightened appreciation for life and everyday experiences.

options.text: Personal strength-1, New possibilities-2, Relating to others-3, Appreciation of life-4
Personal strength-2, New possibilities-1, Relating to others-3, Appreciation of life-4
Personal strength-3, New possibilities-4, Relating to others-1, Appreciation of life-2
Personal strength-4, New possibilities-3, Relating to others-2, Appreciation of life-1

why: Personal strength = greater sense of inner strength and capability (1); New possibilities = recognising new paths and opportunities (2); Relating to others = deepened and more meaningful relationships (3); Appreciation of life = heightened appreciation for life (4).

optWhy.A: Correct: Personal strength-1, New possibilities-2, Relating to others-3, Appreciation of life-4.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: Personal strength-2 wrongly assigns new possibilities to personal strength.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: Personal strength-3 wrongly assigns relationships to personal strength.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: Personal strength-4 wrongly assigns appreciation to personal strength.

stem: A person who, after a trauma, reports a deeper sense of connection to something greater than themselves is reporting which PTGI domain:
why: A deeper sense of connection to something greater than oneself after trauma reflects the spiritual change domain of the PTGI.

optWhy.A: Correct: deeper connection to something greater reflects spiritual change.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: personal strength is about one's own capability.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: new possibilities is about new paths in life.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: appreciation of life is about valuing everyday experiences.

stem: Deliberate rumination in post-traumatic growth refers to:

options.text: Purposeful reflection on the traumatic event to make sense of it.
Avoiding all thoughts of the trauma.

why: Deliberate rumination is purposeful reflection on the traumatic event to make sense of it; intrusive thoughts are unwanted and avoidance is not deliberate reflection.

optWhy.A: Correct: deliberate rumination is purposeful reflection to make sense of the trauma.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: only intrusive thoughts describes intrusive rumination, not deliberate rumination.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: avoiding all thoughts is not deliberate reflection.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: deliberate rumination is a cognitive process, not a reflex.

stem: Post-traumatic growth:

options.text: Can coexist with ongoing distress; growth and distress are not opposites.
Requires the complete absence of distress.

why: Post-traumatic growth can coexist with ongoing distress; growth and distress are not opposites.

optWhy.A: Correct: PTG can coexist with distress; they are not opposites.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: PTG does not require complete absence of distress.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: PTG is distinct from resilience.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: PTG does not happen for everyone.

stem: Resilience differs from post-traumatic growth in that:

options.text: Resilience is maintaining stable functioning after adversity, whereas PTG is positive change beyond pre-trauma functioning following struggle with trauma.
PTG is the same as resilience.
Resilience requires trauma, whereas PTG does not.

why: Resilience is maintaining relatively stable functioning after adversity; PTG is positive change beyond pre-trauma functioning following struggle with trauma.

optWhy.A: Correct: resilience maintains stable functioning; PTG is positive change beyond pre-trauma functioning after struggling with trauma.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: PTG is distinct from resilience.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: resilience does not require trauma.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: PTG does not always follow resilience.

stem: A cancer survivor who, after treatment, reports deeper relationships, a renewed sense of purpose, and greater appreciation of life is demonstrating:
why: Deeper relationships, renewed purpose, and greater appreciation of life after cancer treatment demonstrate post-traumatic growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: deeper relationships, purpose, and appreciation of life reflect post-traumatic growth.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: PTG does not mean cancer is absent.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: PTG involves positive change beyond previous functioning.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: PTG is not guaranteed medical recovery.

stem: An adolescent facing poverty who has a supportive teacher, strong problem-solving skills, and a safe school environment demonstrates protective factors that:

options.text: Guarantee that adversity will not occur.

why: Supportive teacher, problem-solving skills, and safe school are protective factors that can foster resilience despite adversity.

optWhy.A: Correct: these protective factors can foster resilience despite adversity.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: protective factors do not guarantee adversity will not occur.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: protective factors do not eliminate all distress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: protective factors are relevant to outcomes.

stem: Consider the following statements about resilience determinants:
statements: Supportive relationships are a protective factor for resilience.
Individual problem-solving skills contribute to resilience.
Resilience is determined only by genetics.
Community resources can support resilience.
why: Statement 1 is true (supportive relationships are protective); statement 2 is true (problem-solving skills contribute); statement 3 is false (resilience is not only genetic); statement 4 is true (community resources can support resilience).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: Consider the following statements about post-traumatic growth:
statements: PTG can co-occur with ongoing distress.
PTG is the same as resilience.
Deliberate rumination can contribute to PTG.
PTG is guaranteed for all trauma survivors.
why: Statement 1 is true (PTG can co-occur with distress); statement 2 is false (PTG is distinct from resilience); statement 3 is true (deliberate rumination can contribute); statement 4 is false (PTG is not guaranteed).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true; statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 4 is false.

stem: A study compares trauma survivors who engaged in structured written emotional disclosure with a control group that wrote about neutral topics. Six months later, the disclosure group reports greater post-traumatic growth on the PTGI. The best-supported conclusion is:

options.text: Structured written emotional disclosure is associated with greater post-traumatic growth than neutral writing.
Written disclosure guarantees post-traumatic growth for everyone.
Neutral writing produces greater growth than disclosure.
Writing has no effect on growth.

why: The best-supported conclusion is that structured written emotional disclosure is associated with greater post-traumatic growth than neutral writing; it does not show guarantee, that neutral writing is better, or that writing has no effect.

optWhy.A: Correct: disclosure group reported greater PTG than neutral-writing control.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the study does not show guarantee for everyone.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the disclosure group, not neutral writing, showed greater growth.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the disclosure group showed greater growth, so writing had an effect.

stem: Consider the following statements about resilience:
statements: Resilience can be enhanced through supportive relationships and coping skills.
Resilience means never experiencing negative emotions.
Community and family resources contribute to resilience.
Resilience is the same as post-traumatic growth.
why: Statement 1 is true (resilience can be enhanced); statement 2 is false (resilience does not mean never experiencing negative emotions); statement 3 is true (community and family resources contribute); statement 4 is false (resilience is distinct from PTG).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true; statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statements 2 and 4 are false.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 4 is false.

stem: A trauma survivor who receives strong social support and is able to talk openly about the event is more likely to experience:

options.text: Post-traumatic growth, as social support and disclosure are predictors.

why: Strong social support and the ability to talk openly (disclosure) are predictors associated with post-traumatic growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: social support and disclosure are PTG predictors.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: social support can facilitate growth, not only distress.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: growth is not guaranteed.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: trauma occurred.

stem: Consider the following statements about post-traumatic growth and wellbeing:
statements: PTG involves positive psychological change after trauma.
PTG is the same as hedonic wellbeing.
PTG can include renewed appreciation of life.
PTG does not require the absence of distress.
why: Statement 1 is true (PTG is positive change after trauma); statement 2 is false (PTG is not the same as hedonic wellbeing); statement 3 is true (renewed appreciation of life is a PTGI domain); statement 4 is true (PTG does not require absence of distress).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 3, and 4 are true; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 2 is false, and statements 1, 3, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.

stem: An older adult who adapts to retirement and health changes by drawing on lifelong coping skills and social connections demonstrates:

options.text: The absence of any ageing-related change.

why: Drawing on lifelong coping skills and social connections to adapt to ageing-related changes demonstrates resilience across the lifespan.

optWhy.A: Correct: adapting to ageing-related changes using coping skills and social connections is lifespan resilience.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: ageing-related changes occur.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the person adapts rather than only declining.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: resilience is not genetic determinism.

stem: Cultural background can influence post-traumatic growth by shaping:

options.text: How individuals make meaning of trauma and express growth.
The absence of any cultural influence on growth.

why: Cultural background shapes how individuals make meaning of trauma and express growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: cultural background shapes meaning-making and expression of growth.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: cultural considerations are not only biological responses.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: culture does influence growth.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: growth is not a single universal trajectory.

stem: Predictors of post-traumatic growth include:

options.text: Deliberate rumination, social support, and constructive coping.

why: Predictors of PTG include deliberate rumination, social support, and constructive coping; not only genetics, absence of trauma, or income.

optWhy.A: Correct: deliberate rumination, social support, and constructive coping predict PTG.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: PTG is not only genetic inheritance.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: PTG follows trauma, not its absence.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: high income is not the only predictor.

stem: Theories explaining post-traumatic growth include:

options.text: Cognitive processing of the trauma leading to revised assumptions and meaning-making.
The absence of any cognitive processing.

why: Theories explain PTG through cognitive processing of the trauma leading to revised assumptions and meaning-making.

optWhy.A: Correct: cognitive processing leading to revised assumptions and meaning-making explains PTG.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: not only biological changes.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: cognitive processing is central.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: financial compensation is not the explanation.

stem: The relationship among trauma, resilience, coping, and post-traumatic growth is that:

options.text: Coping mediates the trauma–PTG link, and resilience and PTG can co-exist.
PTG requires the absence of coping.

why: Coping mediates the trauma–PTG link, and resilience and PTG can co-exist.

optWhy.A: Correct: coping mediates the trauma–PTG link; resilience and PTG co-exist.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: resilience does not prevent all trauma.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: PTG involves coping, not its absence.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: trauma does not always lead to PTG.

stem: Park's meaning-making model suggests that after trauma, individuals:

options.text: Strive to reconcile the event with their existing beliefs, generating new meaning.

why: Meaning-making involves striving to reconcile the traumatic event with existing beliefs, generating new meaning.

optWhy.A: Correct: meaning-making reconciles the event with beliefs, generating new meaning.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: individuals do reconsider their beliefs.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: individuals do more than only experience distress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: meaning-making requires effort, not automaticity.

stem: A person who, after illness, re-evaluates priorities, strengthens relationships, and pursues valued goals demonstrates:
why: Re-evaluating priorities, strengthening relationships, and pursuing valued goals after illness demonstrate self-growth and flourishing.

optWhy.A: Correct: re-evaluating priorities, relationships, and valued goals reflect self-growth and flourishing.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: self-growth is more than absence of illness.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the person grows rather than only declines.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: self-growth is not genetic determinism.

stem: Protective factors and strengths-based interventions:

options.text: Build on existing strengths and resources to promote wellbeing and resilience.
Only focus on weaknesses and pathology.

why: Protective factors and strengths-based interventions build on existing strengths and resources to promote wellbeing and resilience.

optWhy.A: Correct: they build on existing strengths and resources.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: they focus on strengths, not only weaknesses.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: context matters.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: they do not guarantee immunity.

stem: A person who maintains steady functioning after a bereavement shows resilience; a different person who, after struggling with bereavement, reports new appreciation of life and deeper relationships shows:
why: Steady functioning after bereavement is resilience; new appreciation and deeper relationships after struggling with bereavement are PTG, distinct from resilience.

optWhy.A: Correct: new appreciation and deeper relationships after struggling with bereavement reflect PTG.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: PTG is distinct from resilience.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: PTG is positive change, not only distress.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: bereavement occurred.

stem: After a natural disaster, a community creates a memorial and shared narrative to make sense of the event. This reflects:
why: Creating a memorial and shared narrative reflects collective meaning-making after trauma.

optWhy.A: Correct: memorial and shared narrative reflect collective meaning-making.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the disaster is not forgotten.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: it is collective, not only individual coping.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the disaster occurred.

stem: Consider the following statements about resilience and post-traumatic growth:
statements: Resilience involves maintaining functioning in the face of adversity.
Post-traumatic growth involves positive change beyond pre-trauma functioning.
Resilience and post-traumatic growth cannot occur in the same person.
Coping is relevant to both resilience and post-traumatic growth.
why: Statement 1 is true (resilience maintains functioning); statement 2 is true (PTG is positive change beyond pre-trauma); statement 3 is false (they can co-occur); statement 4 is true (coping is relevant to both).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 2, and 4 are true; statement 3 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 3 is false, and statements 1, 2, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 3 is false.

stem: A study randomly assigns trauma survivors to either a meaning-reconstruction intervention or a waitlist control. Post-intervention, the intervention group reports greater PTG and wellbeing. The best-supported conclusion is:

options.text: Meaning-reconstruction intervention is associated with greater PTG and wellbeing than waitlist.

why: The best-supported conclusion is that meaning-reconstruction intervention is associated with greater PTG and wellbeing than waitlist.

optWhy.A: Correct: intervention group reported greater PTG and wellbeing than waitlist.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: the study does not show guarantee for everyone.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: the intervention group, not waitlist, showed greater PTG.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: the intervention group showed greater PTG, so it had an effect.

stem: Cultural background can shape self-growth by influencing:

options.text: The values and meanings through which growth is understood.
The absence of any cultural influence.

why: Cultural background influences the values and meanings through which self-growth is understood.

optWhy.A: Correct: culture shapes the values and meanings of growth.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: culture is not only biological responses.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: culture influences growth.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: growth is not a single universal path.

stem: Assertion: Post-traumatic growth is not an inevitable outcome of trauma. Reason: Many people experience trauma without reporting post-traumatic growth, and growth co-exists with distress.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

why: Assertion A is true: PTG is not inevitable. Reason R is true: many experience trauma without PTG, and growth co-exists with distress. R correctly explains A.

optWhy.A: Correct: both true; reason explains assertion.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: R is the correct explanation.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: R is true.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: A is true.

stem: Coping in the trauma–post-traumatic growth relationship:

options.text: Can mediate how trauma translates into growth, with constructive coping supporting growth.

why: Coping can mediate how trauma translates into growth, with constructive coping supporting growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: coping mediates trauma-to-growth; constructive coping supports growth.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: coping is relevant to growth.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: coping does not always prevent growth.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: coping is distinct from resilience.

stem: Consider the following statements about wellbeing and self-growth:
statements: Self-growth can enhance wellbeing over time.
Wellbeing is fixed and cannot improve.
Meaning-making contributes to self-growth.
Protective factors support both wellbeing and resilience.
why: Statement 1 is true (self-growth can enhance wellbeing); statement 2 is false (wellbeing is not fixed); statement 3 is true (meaning-making contributes); statement 4 is true (protective factors support wellbeing and resilience).

optWhy.A: Correct: statements 1, 3, and 4 are true; statement 2 is false.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: statement 2 is false, and statements 1, 3, and 4 (true) are omitted.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: statement 2 is false.

stem: A trauma survivor with a tendency toward hopeful, future-oriented thinking shows a predictor associated with:
why: Dispositional optimism is associated with greater likelihood of post-traumatic growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: hopeful future-oriented thinking (optimism) is associated with PTG.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: optimism is associated with growth, not only pessimism.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: growth is not guaranteed.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: trauma occurred.

stem: Personality traits such as openness to experience and extraversion have been linked to:
why: Openness to experience and extraversion are linked to greater likelihood of post-traumatic growth.

optWhy.A: Correct: openness and extraversion are linked to PTG.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: they are linked to growth, not only neuroticism.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: trauma occurred.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: they do not guarantee resilience.

stem: The relationship between trauma severity and post-traumatic growth is best described as:

options.text: Complex: extreme severity can overwhelm coping, while moderate challenge may stimulate growth; not a simple linear relation.
Always linear: greater severity always means more growth.
Always inverse: greater severity always means less growth.

why: Trauma severity and PTG have a complex, non-linear relationship.

optWhy.A: Correct: complex non-linear relation; extreme severity can overwhelm, moderate challenge may stimulate growth.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: not always linear.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: not always inverse.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: there is a relationship.

stem: Constructive coping in the context of trauma includes:

options.text: Problem-solving, emotional regulation, and seeking support.

why: Constructive coping includes problem-solving, emotional regulation, and seeking support.

optWhy.A: Correct: constructive coping includes problem-solving, emotional regulation, seeking support.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: denial and avoidance are not constructive.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: substance use is not constructive coping.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: constructive coping does not guarantee absence of distress.

stem: After trauma, a person revises their assumption that "the world is fair and safe" to a more complex understanding. This reflects:
why: Revising the assumption that the world is fair and safe reflects revised assumptions through meaning-making.

optWhy.A: Correct: revising assumptions reflects meaning-making.
optWhy.B: Incorrect: trauma occurred.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: denial is not meaning-making.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: meaning-making does not guarantee recovery.

stem: Self-growth is closely linked to:

options.text: Eudaimonic wellbeing, including meaning, purpose, and self-realisation.

why: Self-growth is closely linked to eudaimonic wellbeing.

optWhy.A: Correct: self-growth links to eudaimonic wellbeing (meaning, purpose, self-realisation).
optWhy.B: Incorrect: not only hedonic pleasure.
optWhy.C: Incorrect: not only financial wealth.
optWhy.D: Incorrect: self-growth is growth, not absence.

stem: Consider the following statements about protective factors, resilience, and PTG:
statements: Social support is a protective factor for both resilience and post-traumatic growth.
Protective factors guarantee that trauma will not occur.
